case.case_title: Cannosa Investments Limited v. Earnest Perera and Others
case.source_citation: Supreme Court of Sri Lanka, S.C. Application 12/90, decided on 10 October 1990

clause.text: No person shall be arrested except according to law and must be informed of the reason.

case_context.legal_issue: Whether the petitioner was informed of the reason for arrest and whether the fundamental right under Article 13(1) was violated.
case_context.petitioner_claim: The petitioner alleged that persons were taken into custody unlawfully and without proper legal basis, and that the police acted mala fide in executing a search warrant obtained improperly.
case_context.respondent_argument: The respondents argued that the police acted in obedience to a judicial order (search warrant) and thus their actions did not constitute executive or administrative action violating fundamental rights under Article 126.
key_facts: Police entered the casino premises on 6 April 1990 with a search warrant.
The Magistrate admitted issuing the search warrant inadvertently without complying with Section 5(1) of the Gaming Ordinance.
Petitioner claimed the police acted mala fide and for collateral purposes.
The Magistrate acted honestly and in purported exercise of jurisdiction.
The question whether the police informed detainees of the reason for arrest was relevant.

reasoning.interpretation_summary: The Court held that the violation of Article 13(1) requires that a person be informed of the reason for arrest. In this case, the petitioner did not obtain relief under Article 13(1) because the arrest and detention were consequences of a judicial order, which is outside the scope of Article 126. The Court emphasized that judicial acts, even if maliciously obtained, do not constitute executive or administrative action violating fundamental rights under Article 126.
reasoning.application_to_facts: The Court found that the police acted pursuant to a judicial order (search warrant) and that the Magistrate was not shown to have acted mala fide. Therefore, the police action was not executive or administrative action violating Article 13(1). The petitioner was not entitled to relief under Article 13(1) for failure to inform of the reason for arrest in this context.
principles_established: Judicial orders, even if maliciously obtained, do not attract liability under Article 126.
Police officers acting in obedience to judicial orders are immune from fundamental rights claims if acting in good faith.
Article 13(1) protects the right to be informed of the reason for arrest, but this does not extend to acts done pursuant to judicial orders.

outcome.holding: The application under Article 13(1) was dismissed as the police action was pursuant to a judicial order and did not constitute a violation of the right to be informed of the reason for arrest.

link_explanation.why_this_clause_matters: Article 13(1) was central to the petitioner's claim that persons were arrested without being informed of the reason, but the Court found that the police acted under a judicial order, thus excluding the claim under this clause.

evidence.evidence_excerpt: The petitioner alleged persons were taken into custody without proper legal basis and not informed of the reason, but the Court held the police acted pursuant to a judicial order and no violation of Article 13(1) occurred.
